name: Mesoamerican peoples outside the Aztec Empire
summary: The many Mesoamerican peoples and states not ruled by the Aztecs in 1519, such as the Purépecha (Tarascan) Empire, Tlaxcala, the Mixtec kingdom of Tututepec, Zapotec, Totonac and others; Tlaxcala helped Cortés defeat the Aztecs.

location.value: Central and southern Mexico, Belize, Guatemala and also El Salvador, western Honduras and Greater Nicoya, between about 10° and 22° N.

terrain.value: Volcanic highlands and lake basins such as Pátzcuaro, the mountain valleys of Oaxaca, and hot coastal lowlands.

climate.value: Varied: cool highlands and hot, humid coasts, with a rainy season from about May to October.

resources.value: Maize, beans and squash, cotton, cacao from the Pacific coast, copper in western Mexico, and obsidian for tools.

disasters.value: Earthquakes, volcanic activity, droughts and crop failures; frosts could ruin highland maize harvests.

population.value: The Tarascan state's infobox gives 1,500,000 people in 1519. Totals for other peoples are not given.

urbanisation.value: Cities such as Tzintzuntzan and Tlaxcala.

disease.value: Smallpox spread from 1520, killing many, including the Purépecha ruler Zuangua.

migration.value: Groups from the north, such as Chichimecs, moved south; Purépecha legends tell of founders arriving at Lake Pátzcuaro.

economicBase.value: The Tarascans were the foremost metalworkers in pre-Conquest Mexico, and tribute from conquered areas was shared among lords and nobles. Farming and markets are not covered.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade in cacao, cotton, salt, obsidian and feathers; the Aztec blockade cut Tlaxcala off from salt and cotton.

wealth.value: Rulers and nobles gained wealth from tribute in cloth, maize and luxury goods, and from long-distance trade.

moneyAndTax.value: Cacao beans and cotton cloth were used as money; copper axe-shaped pieces circulated in western Mexico and Oaxaca.

inequality.value: Mostly small-scale societies; some ranked chiefs and families.

governmentType.value: A monarchy: a network of tributary systems that became more centralised. Tlaxcala was not checked.

keyRulers.value: Tangáxuan II, the last independent ruler (about 1520–30), submitted to the Spanish and was executed by Nuño de Guzmán on 14 February 1530. Xicotencatl is not checked.

succession.value: Rule passed within royal and noble lineages, with councils of nobles taking part in choices.

institutions.value: The Purépecha ruler (cazonci) with priests and governors; Tlaxcala’s council of nobles from its four parts.

stability.value: Long wars against the Aztecs: “flower wars” with Tlaxcala and a fortified frontier with the Purépecha.

eliteConflict.value: Rival lords and city-states competed for land and tribute, especially among the Mixtec and Zapotec.

armyAndTech.value: Obsidian-edged clubs, bows and cotton armour; Purépecha smiths made copper and bronze tools and ornaments.

majorWars.value: In the 1470s Aztec forces under Axayacatl were defeated (the page gives no 1479 date). The Tarascan kingdom lost its independence to the Spanish in 1530.

territoryChange.value: Conquered by Spain: Tututepec and the Purépecha in 1522, Oaxaca soon after and Guatemala from 1524.

alliancesRivals.value: Tlaxcala and Huejotzingo were enemies of the Aztecs; Tlaxcala allied with Cortés in 1519.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled local technologies.

scienceEducation.value: A 260-day ritual calendar and 365-day year; Mixtec screenfold books such as the Codex Zouche-Nuttall.

openness.value: Trade and exchange with neighbours through markets and merchants, despite frequent wars.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths with human porters (no wheeled transport or pack animals), and canoes on lakes and rivers.

religion.value: Polytheist, worshipping many gods called Tukúpacha; the page names Kweráwahpiri and does not name Curicaueri.

languageWriting.value: One of only five regions where writing developed independently, with mostly logosyllabic scripts; a 260-day ritual calendar and a 365-day solar calendar.

artsArchitecture.value: Yácatas pyramids at Tzintzuntzan, stone mosaics at Mitla and Mixtec gold jewellery and painted codices.

socialStructure.value: Rulers and nobles, priests, merchants and craftworkers, farming commoners, and some slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Identity rested on each people, village and language rather than one state.

dailyLife.value: Families grew maize, beans and chilli, ground maize for tortillas and wove cotton or maguey cloth.

neighbours.value: The Aztec Empire in central Mexico, Maya kingdoms in Yucatán and Guatemala, and Chichimec peoples to the north.

ideasReligions.value: The shared Mesoamerican calendar, ball game and sacrifice, followed by Christian missions after the conquest.

colonisation.value: Spanish conquest (1519–25), followed by colonial rule as part of New Spain.

riseSignals.value: The Olmec, the first complex civilisation in Mesoamerica, occupied their main sites from roughly 1200 to 400 BCE; the earliest maize at Guilá Naquitz, Oaxaca, dates to c. 4000 BCE. The Postclassic began 900–1000 CE depending on area (table: 900–1519).

peakPeriod.value: By about 1450 the Uacúsecha led an empire of 75,000 km² in west Mexico; at the Spanish conquest it was the second-largest state in Mesoamerica.

declineSignals.value: Spanish conquest from 1519 and epidemics such as smallpox that killed large numbers of people.

outcome.value: The Postclassic ended with the Spanish conquest of the Aztecs between 1519 and 1521; Eurasian diseases caused upwards of 90% of Indigenous deaths after contact.

overallCertainty.value: Known from archaeology, oral history and Spanish and later records; population figures are estimates.
